text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, A35 led into a three-activity cluster — A15, A17 and A18, each running in essentially every trace in varying order — which always exited to A20, while A24 led into exactly one of A14, A16 or A19, which always exited to A25. In the later window this is reversed: A35 leads into exactly one of A14, A16 or A19, which always exits to A20, and A24 leads into the A15/A17/A18 cluster, which now always exits to A25. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, DIR006, DIR007, DIR008]
- Every measured activity pair spanning the two segments reversed its order. A15 preceded A20 in all 200 earlier traces and follows it in all later traces; A24 preceded A14 in the 31 in 100 earlier traces containing A14, whereas A14 now precedes A24 in the 44 in 100 later traces containing it; A17 moved from always preceding A24 to always following it. [REL001, REL005, REL008, REL009, REL015, REL016, REL020]
- The spacing between the anchor activities flipped accordingly: A25 followed A24 two event positions later in the earlier window and four positions later in the later window, while A20 followed A35 four positions later earlier and two positions later afterwards — the one-activity and three-activity segments swapped sides around A20 and A24, which keep their places between them. [LAG001, LAG002, REL008, REL009, REL012, REL016]
- Within the single-step segment, the choice shifted toward A14: it runs in about 44 of 100 later traces versus about 31 of 100 earlier, while A16 (about 38 down to 29 in 100) and A19 (about 32 down to 28 in 100) are chosen less often; the three shares still sum to one such step per trace. [OCC001, DIR003, DIR006, DIR008]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that two segments exchanged their places. In the earlier window the sequence ran A35, then the A15/A17/A18 cluster, then the anchors A20 and A24, then exactly one of A14/A16/A19, then A25; in the later window the single A14/A16/A19 step runs first (fed by A35, exiting to A20) and the A15/A17/A18 cluster runs last (fed by A24, exiting to A25). A14, A16 and A19 each changed their predecessor from A24 to A35 and their successor from A25 to A20; A15, A17 and A18 changed their collective entry from A35 to A24 and their exit from A20 to A25. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, DIR006, DIR007, DIR008]

This is shown directly by relational and positional evidence rather than inferred from frequencies: all cross-segment pairs reverse order, and the A24→A25 and A35→A20 distances flip between two and four positions, matching the two segments swapping sides. The change is consistent across all 32 qualifying items (about 0.4 would be expected by chance for the 83 control-flow units tested), each difference exceeding about 995 of 1000 random re-splits, and competing explanations are largely excluded: every involved activity is well observed in both windows (cluster members and anchors in essentially all traces; A14, A16, A19 in 28–44 in 100), and neither ordering leaks into the other window (0 of 200 traces each). Note that the many pair-level items describe one underlying rearrangement, not independent changes. [LAG001, LAG002, REL001, REL008, REL015, REL020, DIR001, DIR002, OCC001]

Limitations: the evidence cannot distinguish a single simultaneous exchange of the two segments from two separate relocations, and it cannot rule out that the later ordering existed earlier as a rare variant that the 200 earlier traces did not capture; the internal order of the A15/A17/A18 cluster remains flexible in both windows, so the change concerns where the blocks sit, not a fixed permutation of individual activities. [REL008, REL015, REL018, DIR002, DIR004, DIR005]

Other differences: within the single-step segment, routing shares moved toward A14 (about 31 to 44 in 100 traces) at the expense of A16 (about 38 to 29) and A19 (about 32 to 28); all three alternatives remain in use, so this is a shift between existing paths rather than a replacement. [OCC001, DIR003, DIR006, DIR008]
